title: Counting Square Roots of Unity mod n: the Odd Case 2^ω(n)

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: sqrtOneCount: the counting function N(n) = #{x : ZMod n | x² = 1}, the number of square roots of unity modulo n
sq_eq_one_iff_prime_pow: elementary local classification — in ZMod (p^k) with p an odd prime, x² = 1 ↔ x = 1 ∨ x = -1, proved via the coprimality of (a-1) and (a+1) rather than cyclic-group structure
sqrtOneCount_prime_pow: the local count N(p^k) = 2 for every odd prime power
sqrtOneCount_mul: multiplicativity N(m·n) = N(m)·N(n) for coprime m, n, transported across the CRT ring isomorphism ZMod (m·n) ≃+* ZMod m × ZMod n
sqrtOneCount_odd: the headline result — for odd n, N(n) = 2^ω(n) where ω(n) = n.primeFactors.card, assembled from multiplicativity via Nat.multiplicative_factorization

description: Counts the square roots of unity modulo an odd n. For N(n) = #{x : ZMod n | x² = 1}, proves N(n) = 2^ω(n), where ω(n) is the number of distinct prime factors. The argument is elementary and structural: at each odd prime power p^k the only solutions of x² = 1 are ±1 (because p, being odd, cannot divide both x−1 and x+1), giving N(p^k) = 2; the Chinese Remainder Theorem makes N multiplicative; and Nat.multiplicative_factorization assembles the product 2·2·…·2 = 2^ω(n) over the distinct primes.

overview.historicalContext: Counting the square roots of unity modulo n is the arithmetic core of Gauss's generalization of Wilson's theorem. Wilson's theorem (stated by John Wilson, first proved by Lagrange in 1771) says (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for prime p. In the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801, art. 78) Gauss extended this to a general modulus: the product of all units of ℤ/n is ≡ −1 when n = 1, 2, 4, p^k, or 2p^k for an odd prime p, and ≡ +1 otherwise. The reason is purely group-theoretic — in a finite abelian group the product of all elements equals the product of its involutions — so the sign is decided by the 2-torsion of (ℤ/n)ˣ, i.e. by exactly the square roots of unity counted here. The count itself is governed by the structure theorem for (ℤ/n)ˣ: for an odd prime power p^k the group is cyclic of even order p^{k−1}(p−1), contributing a single order-2 element (the two roots ±1), while the prime 2 is anomalous — (ℤ/2^k)ˣ ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2^{k−2} for k ≥ 3 is non-cyclic, the sole source of extra involutions (a Klein four-group of square roots). This entry treats the clean odd case, where every prime contributes a factor of 2 and N(n) = 2^{ω(n)}. The function ω(n) counting distinct prime factors is itself a classical object, whose normal order log log n (Hardy–Ramanujan, 1917) and Gaussian fluctuations (Erdős–Kac, 1940) are landmarks of probabilistic number theory.
overview.problemStatement: The parent studies the 2-torsion of $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$ — the square roots of unity — and asks for the exact count $N(n) = \#\{x : x^2 = 1\}$ in the form $2^{\omega_{\mathrm{odd}}(n)+\delta}$, where $\omega_{\mathrm{odd}}$ counts odd prime factors and $\delta\in\{0,1,2\}$ is a 2-adic correction. This entry resolves the odd-modulus case, where $\delta = 0$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{odd}}(n) = \omega(n)$: for odd $n$, $N(n) = 2^{\omega(n)}$.
overview.proofStrategy: Work with roots of unity in the ring $\mathbb{Z}/n$ (a solution of $x^2=1$ is automatically a unit, so this counts the same set), in three steps. (1) A self-contained elementary proof that $\mathbb{Z}/p^k$ has exactly the two square roots $\pm 1$ for odd $p$ (`sq_eq_one_iff_prime_pow`), via the coprimality of $(x-1)$ and $(x+1)$ rather than any cyclic-group structure, giving the local count $N(p^k)=2$ (`sqrtOneCount_prime_pow`). (2) The Chinese Remainder Theorem transports $x^2=1$ componentwise, so $N$ is multiplicative on coprime arguments. (3) The standard multiplicative-function factorization collapses the product over the prime factorization to $\prod_{p\mid n} 2 = 2^{\omega(n)}$.
keyInsights: The number of square roots of unity mod n is a group-theoretic fingerprint of (ℤ/n)ˣ: it equals the order of the 2-torsion subgroup #(ℤ/n)ˣ[2], so counting them measures the 2-rank of the unit group. By the structure theorem this is 2 raised to the number of cyclic factors of even order.

The elementary heart of the odd case is that an odd prime cannot divide two integers differing by 2. From p^k ∣ (a−1)(a+1) with p odd, coprimality of the factors forces p^k entirely into one of them, so x ≡ 1 or x ≡ −1 — no cyclic-generator or primitive-root machinery is needed.

Multiplicativity is not a lucky coincidence but the Chinese Remainder Theorem in action: the solution set of any fixed polynomial congruence factors through ℤ/(mn) ≅ ℤ/m × ℤ/n, so N is a genuine multiplicative arithmetic function. The same argument counts roots of any polynomial multiplicatively.

All deviation from 2^{ω(n)} is 2-adic in origin. The prime 2 is the unique anomaly: (ℤ/2^k)ˣ is cyclic for k ≤ 2 but ℤ/2 × ℤ/2^{k−2} for k ≥ 3, producing a Klein four-group of square roots. Removing the even part (δ = 0) isolates the clean odd formula and pins the full correction 2^{ω_odd(n)+δ} on the single prime 2.

This count governs the sign in Gauss's generalization of Wilson's theorem: the product of all units of ℤ/n equals the product of its involutions, which is −1 exactly when there is a unique nontrivial square root of unity (N(n) = 2) and +1 otherwise. So N(n) is the quantity deciding the Wilson product's sign.

N(n) = 2^{ω(n)} exhibits the arithmetic function ω(n) — the number of distinct prime factors — in a concrete counting role. On odd n the count therefore inherits ω's celebrated statistics: normal order log log n (Hardy–Ramanujan) and asymptotic normality (Erdős–Kac).

The formalization packages N as literally satisfying the hypotheses of Nat.multiplicative_factorization (N(1) = 1 and multiplicativity on coprimes), so the collapse of the product over the prime factorization to 2^{ω(n)} becomes a short, structural calculation rather than an induction written by hand.
overview.problem: The parent entry studies the 2-torsion of (ZMod n)ˣ — the square roots of unity. Its open question asks for the exact count N(n) = #{x : x² = 1} in the form 2^(ω_odd(n) + δ), where ω_odd counts odd prime factors and δ ∈ {0,1,2} is a 2-adic correction. This entry resolves the odd-modulus case, where δ = 0 and ω_odd(n) = ω(n).
overview.approach: Work with roots of unity in the ring ZMod n (a root of x²=1 is automatically a unit, so this counts the same set). Three steps: (1) a self-contained elementary proof that ZMod (p^k) has exactly the two square roots ±1 for odd p; (2) CRT transports x²=1 componentwise, so N is multiplicative on coprime arguments; (3) the standard multiplicative-function factorization collapses the product over the prime factorization to 2^ω(n).
overview.significance: Gives a fully verified, axiom-free count for the odd case using an elementary coprimality argument rather than the cyclic-group machinery of the parent, and packages N as a genuine multiplicative arithmetic function. It isolates exactly what the 2-adic prime contributes (the δ correction) by removing it.

conclusion.summary: For odd n, the number of square roots of unity modulo n is exactly 2^ω(n), where ω(n) = n.primeFactors.card. 182 lines, 6 theorems, 1 definition, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. The count N is built as a multiplicative arithmetic function: N(p^k) = 2 at every odd prime power (elementary ±1 classification), N is multiplicative via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and Nat.multiplicative_factorization assembles 2^ω(n).
conclusion.implications: This is the δ = 0 slice of the parent's open question 2^(ω_odd(n)+δ). By handling the odd case with a clean elementary argument, it makes precise that all of the non-2^ω behavior in the general formula is 2-adic in origin: the factor of 2, 4 (Klein four-group) refinements only appear from the prime 2. The multiplicative packaging also directly recovers classical facts such as N(n) = 2 iff n is 1, 2, or an odd prime power times at most one factor of 2.
openQuestions: The 2-adic completion: extend to all n by computing N(2^k) = 1, 2, 4 for k = 1, 2, ≥3 (the Klein four-group (ZMod 2^k)ˣ[2] for k ≥ 3) and combining with the odd part to obtain the full 2^(ω_odd(n)+δ) formula.
The dual Gauss–Wilson product: relate N(n) to the value of the product of all units of ZMod n (the generalized Wilson theorem), whose sign is governed by whether N(n) = 2.

sections.title: Statement and Strategy
sections.summary: Imports and the overview docstring: the goal N(n) = 2^ω(n) for odd n as the δ = 0 slice of the parent's open question, plus the three-step plan (local ±1 count, CRT multiplicativity, factorization assembly).

sections.title: Definition and Base Case
sections.summary: Defines sqrtOneCount n = Nat.card {x : ZMod n // x² = 1} and proves the multiplicative normalization N(1) = 1 via the subsingleton structure of the zero ring ZMod 1.

sections.title: Odd Prime Power: Only ±1
sections.summary: The elementary coprimality argument: in ZMod (p^k) for odd p, x² = 1 ↔ x = ±1 (an odd p cannot divide both a−1 and a+1), together with the distinctness lemma 1 ≠ -1 that keeps the count at two.

sections.title: Local Count N(p^k) = 2
sections.summary: Assembles the classification and distinctness into the two-element Finset {1, -1}, giving N(p^k) = 2 for every odd prime power via Finset.card_pair.

sections.title: CRT Multiplicativity
sections.summary: For coprime m, n, transports x² = 1 across the Chinese Remainder isomorphism ZMod (m·n) ≃+* ZMod m × ZMod n and splits componentwise to prove N(m·n) = N(m)·N(n).

sections.title: Main Theorem: N(n) = 2^ω(n)
sections.summary: Nat.multiplicative_factorization writes N(n) as the product of local counts over the prime factorization; every prime of an odd n is odd, so each factor is 2 and the product collapses to 2^ω(n).
